The design handoff's U.S.-Iran sample copy is illustrative only and its own README says it must not ship as fact; PRD 07 would also require senior review for casualty and attribution claims, and there is no editorial team. Same ten sections, a fraction of the risk.

concepts.title: Appropriation
concepts.shortGloss: A law letting an agency spend a specific amount for a specific purpose.
concepts.plainDefinition: An appropriation is an act of Congress that provides legal authority for a federal agency to incur obligations and to make payments from the Treasury for a stated purpose, up to a stated amount, within a stated period.
concepts.whyItMatters: Without an appropriation an agency cannot legally spend, no matter how popular the program or how clearly another law authorizes it. This is why a programme can exist on paper and still have no money.
concepts.currentExample: The twelve regular appropriations bills that fund the federal government each fiscal year.
concepts.commonMisunderstanding: That authorizing a program and funding it are the same act. They are two different bills, often passed years apart, and sometimes only one of them ever happens.
concepts.tryItQuestion: A bill creating a new agency passes. Can the agency hire anyone?
concepts.confusionDiscriminator: An authorization says a program may exist; an appropriation says money may be spent on it.

concepts.title: Authorization
concepts.shortGloss: A law establishing a program and setting a spending ceiling — not the money itself.
concepts.plainDefinition: An authorization establishes, continues or modifies a federal program or agency and typically sets a maximum amount that may later be appropriated to it. It does not by itself provide any funds.
concepts.whyItMatters: Coverage frequently reports an authorization figure as though the money is committed. It is a ceiling on a future decision, not a transfer.
concepts.currentExample: An annual defense authorization act, which sets policy and ceilings but appropriates nothing.
concepts.commonMisunderstanding: That an authorized dollar figure is money that has been provided.
concepts.tryItQuestion: A bill authorizes $10 billion over five years. How much has been spent?
concepts.confusionDiscriminator: An authorization says a program may exist; an appropriation says money may be spent on it.

concepts.title: Obligation
concepts.shortGloss: A binding commitment to pay — signing the contract, not sending the cheque.
concepts.plainDefinition: An obligation is a definite commitment by a federal agency that creates a legal liability to pay, such as signing a contract or issuing a grant award. The payment itself follows later.
concepts.whyItMatters: Obligation is the stage where money stops being available for anything else. It is also the first stage that appears in public spending data, which is why so much reporting starts here.
concepts.currentExample: An agency awarding a construction contract; the funds are obligated on award, and outlaid as the work is invoiced.
concepts.commonMisunderstanding: That obligated money has been spent. The cash may leave the Treasury months or years later, and some of it never does.
concepts.tryItQuestion: A contract is signed in September and paid the following June. In which year was the money obligated?
concepts.confusionDiscriminator: An obligation is the promise to pay; an outlay is the money actually leaving the Treasury.

concepts.title: Outlay
concepts.plainDefinition: An outlay is a payment made to liquidate an obligation — the point at which federal cash actually leaves the Treasury.
concepts.whyItMatters: This is the only stage at which the government has, in plain language, spent the money. Every earlier stage is a form of intention.
concepts.currentExample: A Treasury disbursement against an invoice on an already-obligated contract.
concepts.commonMisunderstanding: That the headline figure in a spending story is an outlay. Usually it is a request or an appropriation, four or five stages earlier.
concepts.tryItQuestion: Which of requested, appropriated and outlaid means the money is gone?
concepts.confusionDiscriminator: An obligation is the promise to pay; an outlay is the money actually leaving the Treasury.

concepts.title: Continuing resolution
concepts.shortGloss: A stopgap law funding agencies at existing levels when the regular bills are late.
concepts.plainDefinition: A continuing resolution is an appropriation that funds agencies at or near their prior-year levels for a limited period, used when Congress has not enacted the regular appropriations bills before the fiscal year begins.
concepts.whyItMatters: It keeps agencies open, but it also freezes funding to last year's priorities and makes multi-year planning difficult.
concepts.currentExample: A short-term measure carrying agencies past October 1 while negotiations continue.
concepts.commonMisunderstanding: That a continuing resolution is a failure to fund the government. It is a real appropriation — just a temporary and backward-looking one.
concepts.tryItQuestion: Under a continuing resolution, can an agency start a new program it just received authorization for?

concepts.title: Antideficiency Act
concepts.shortGloss: The law making it illegal to spend or commit money Congress has not appropriated.
concepts.plainDefinition: A group of statutes, principally 31 U.S.C. § 1341, prohibiting federal officers from obligating or expending funds in excess of, or in advance of, an appropriation.
concepts.whyItMatters: It is the reason a lapse in appropriations produces a shutdown rather than an IOU: without an appropriation, continuing to obligate is not merely unfunded, it is unlawful.
concepts.currentExample: Agencies furloughing non-excepted staff when appropriations lapse.
concepts.commonMisunderstanding: That agencies shut down because they run out of cash. They stop because continuing to obligate would be illegal.
concepts.tryItQuestion: Why can't an agency keep operating on credit during a funding lapse?

concepts.title: Stopgap funding
concepts.shortGloss: A temporary bill that keeps agencies open at last year's levels.
concepts.plainDefinition: A continuing resolution extends the previous year's funding levels for a fixed number of days or weeks so agencies can keep operating while Congress finishes the twelve regular bills. It is a deadline extension, not a budget.
concepts.whyItMatters: A stopgap freezes last year's priorities in place. New programs cannot start, and agencies plan in the length of the extension rather than the length of the year.
concepts.currentExample: The House passed a stopgap on 22 July 2026 with the Senate's vote uncertain; a separate Senate deal followed on 2 August.
concepts.commonMisunderstanding: That passing a continuing resolution means Congress passed a budget. It means the opposite -- the budget is not done.
concepts.tryItQuestion: If a stopgap holds funding at last year's level, what happens to a program Congress voted to expand this year?
concepts.confusionDiscriminator: An appropriation sets new amounts for the year ahead. A continuing resolution copies forward the amounts already in force.

concepts.title: Rescission
concepts.shortGloss: Congress cancelling budget authority it already granted.
concepts.plainDefinition: A rescission takes back spending authority that has already been enacted, before the money is obligated. Because it undoes a law, it takes another law.
concepts.whyItMatters: It is the difference between money never granted and money granted then withdrawn. Coverage often calls both a cut.
concepts.currentExample: The $1.8 billion DOJ 'anti-weaponization' fund was removed from pending legislation on 3 August 2026 -- a fund dropped before enactment, which is not a rescission.
concepts.commonMisunderstanding: That any reduction is a rescission. Dropping a proposal is not rescinding an appropriation.
concepts.tryItQuestion: A committee removes a program from a bill that has not passed. Has anything been rescinded?
concepts.confusionDiscriminator: Rescission is Congress taking money back by law. Impoundment is the executive declining to spend money Congress already provided.

concepts.title: Impoundment
concepts.shortGloss: The executive branch withholding money Congress appropriated.
concepts.plainDefinition: Impoundment is a refusal or delay by the executive branch in spending funds that Congress has appropriated. The Impoundment Control Act of 1974 requires the President to notify Congress and, for permanent cancellations, to obtain its approval.
concepts.whyItMatters: It decides whether an appropriation is an instruction or a ceiling -- the single largest unresolved question about who actually controls federal spending.
concepts.currentExample: Over $800 million in California Medicaid funds was withheld by CMS in July 2026, and the Senate moved on 3 August to limit White House control over federal science funding.
concepts.commonMisunderstanding: That the executive must spend every appropriated dollar immediately. Some delay is routine and lawful; the dispute is about permanent withholding.
concepts.tryItQuestion: Congress appropriates $800M and the agency does not release it. Which stage of the ladder has stalled?
concepts.confusionDiscriminator: Apportionment is the ordinary, scheduled release of funds. Impoundment is withholding beyond that schedule.

concepts.title: Apportionment
concepts.shortGloss: OMB releasing appropriated money to agencies in instalments.
concepts.plainDefinition: After an appropriation is enacted, OMB apportions the funds -- releasing them to agencies by time period or activity so the money is not spent all at once. Agencies cannot obligate funds that have not been apportioned.
concepts.whyItMatters: It is the invisible step between Appropriated and Obligated, and the lever an administration uses to slow spending without saying it is doing so.
concepts.currentExample: Senate action on 3 August 2026 to limit White House control over federal science funding is a dispute about this step.
concepts.commonMisunderstanding: That enactment puts money in an agency's hands. Enactment creates authority; apportionment releases it.
concepts.tryItQuestion: Where in the five stages would a delay be invisible in the headline number?
concepts.confusionDiscriminator: Apportionment is OMB releasing funds to an agency. Obligation is the agency committing them to someone outside government.

concepts.title: Supplemental appropriation
concepts.shortGloss: Extra funding requested outside the twelve regular bills.
concepts.plainDefinition: A supplemental provides additional budget authority during a year already under way, usually for something unforeseen -- a disaster, or a military operation that outran its budget.
concepts.whyItMatters: Supplementals are where wartime costs usually appear, and they bypass the ordinary committee calendar that gives the public time to see a number coming.
concepts.currentExample: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth submitted a classified supplemental request to Congress on 5 August 2026.
concepts.commonMisunderstanding: That a supplemental is a smaller or lesser kind of funding. Supplementals have carried some of the largest single appropriations in U.S. history.
concepts.tryItQuestion: If a request is classified, which of the five stages can the public still verify?
concepts.confusionDiscriminator: Both are appropriations. A supplemental is simply one enacted mid-year, on top of what was already provided.

concepts.title: Budget reconciliation
concepts.shortGloss: A filibuster-proof track for certain budget legislation.
concepts.plainDefinition: Reconciliation lets specified budget legislation pass the Senate with a simple majority and limited debate, provided a budget resolution has instructed committees to produce it and the contents survive the Byrd rule.
concepts.whyItMatters: It is how a single party can enact major fiscal policy without the other party's votes -- and why a budget blueprint that looks procedural is often the substantive move.
concepts.currentExample: The House passed a budget blueprint alongside the Pentagon bill on 22 July 2026 designed to unlock reconciliation.
concepts.commonMisunderstanding: That reconciliation is an appropriations process. It is not -- appropriations bills are not reconciliation bills.
concepts.tryItQuestion: Why would a majority pass a budget blueprint before it has agreed on the policy it intends to pass?
concepts.confusionDiscriminator: Appropriations provide money for the year. Reconciliation is a procedural track, mostly for mandatory spending and revenue.

actors.name: House Committee on Appropriations
actors.actualPower: Originates the twelve regular appropriations bills and sets the subcommittee allocations that cap each one.
actors.constrainedBy: Must clear the full House, the Senate and the President; bound by any statutory spending caps in force.
actors.statedWants: The committee's published purpose is to set discretionary spending levels through the twelve annual bills.
actors.leverageStatement: Writes the bill text that every later stage either accepts or amends.
actors.roleHere: Originating chamber for appropriations under the Origination Clause practice.

decisions.leverageStatement: Writes the defense bill's text and its topline.
Passed a stopgap on 22 July; a full-year bill has not moved.
Would have had to accept the provision in conference; never got the chance.
Wrote the appropriation. Writing it did not make it move.

actors.name: Senate Committee on Appropriations
actors.actualPower: Marks up its own versions of the twelve bills and negotiates the final text in conference.
actors.constrainedBy: Senate floor procedure, including the cloture threshold on most legislation.
actors.leverageStatement: Can block or rewrite any House-passed appropriation.
actors.roleHere: The second of the two chambers that must agree on identical text.

decisions.leverageStatement: Must pass its own version and reconcile; the House number is not final.
The stopgap's fate in the Senate was still uncertain when both chambers left.
The fund lived or died in the spending legislation it was attached to.
Same -- authority to appropriate is not authority to disburse.

actors.name: Office of Management and Budget
actors.actualPower: Prepares the President's budget request and apportions enacted appropriations to agencies, controlling the rate at which funds become available.
actors.constrainedBy: Cannot spend money Congress has not appropriated, and impoundment is limited by the 1974 Act.
actors.statedWants: Its statutory role is to apportion appropriations so as to prevent deficiencies.
actors.leverageStatement: Controls apportionment, so it sets the pace at which appropriated money becomes usable.
actors.roleHere: The bridge between an enacted appropriation and an agency's ability to obligate.

decisions.leverageStatement: Transmits the request and will apportion whatever is enacted.
Issues the lapse guidance that decides which staff are excepted and which stop.
Apportionment is where a withholding upstream of the agency would be visible.

actors.name: Congressional Budget Office
actors.actualPower: Produces the official cost estimates Congress uses to score legislation.
actors.constrainedBy: Advisory only — it scores bills, it does not decide them.
actors.statedWants: Established by the 1974 Act to give Congress budget information independent of the executive branch.
actors.leverageStatement: Its score frames what a bill is publicly understood to cost.
actors.roleHere: The source of the official cost estimate, where one exists.

decisions.leverageStatement: Scores the bill, which sets the terms the argument is conducted in.

actors.name: Government Accountability Office
actors.actualPower: Issues legal decisions on appropriations law and audits how funds were used.
actors.constrainedBy: Reports and opines; enforcement rests elsewhere.
actors.leverageStatement: Rules after the fact on whether a use of funds was lawful.
actors.roleHere: The authority on what the stages mean, via the Red Book.

decisions.leverageStatement: Can rule on whether an agency-created fund rests on an appropriation.
Can issue a legal decision on whether the withholding is an impoundment requiring notice to Congress.

actors.name: Federal agencies
actors.actualPower: Obligate and outlay appropriated funds within the purpose, time and amount limits set by law.
actors.constrainedBy: The Antideficiency Act, apportionment, and the purpose/time/amount rules.
actors.leverageStatement: Decide the operational detail, but only inside limits set several stages earlier.
actors.roleHere: Where an appropriation finally becomes an obligation and then a payment.

decisions.leverageStatement: Plan for a lapse they cannot prevent; the Antideficiency Act dictates what stops.

actors.name: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense
actors.actualPower: Submits the Department of Defense budget request and supplemental requests, and directs how appropriated defense funds are obligated once released.
actors.constrainedBy: Cannot obligate funds Congress has not appropriated; the Antideficiency Act makes doing so a personal legal exposure, not a policy dispute.
actors.statedWants: Submitted a classified supplemental funding request to Congress seeking additional Department of Defense funds.
actors.leverageStatement: Sets the opening number the whole defense debate negotiates against.
actors.roleHere: Requests defense funding and reports what has been spent; both roles appear in this window.

decisions.leverageStatement: Sets the opening number, including a classified supplemental Congress cannot discuss in public.

actors.name: Senate Majority and Minority Leaders
actors.actualPower: Control floor time, which decides whether a funding bill gets a vote before the deadline.
actors.constrainedBy: Sixty votes for most appropriations business, so neither leader can move a bill without some of the other side.
actors.statedWants: Announced a bipartisan agreement intended to keep the federal government funded and prevent a shutdown.
actors.leverageStatement: A funding bill that never reaches the floor fails without a vote being taken.
actors.roleHere: Negotiated the early-August agreement that is currently the main thing standing between the calendar and a lapse.

decisions.leverageStatement: Controls whether the bill reaches the floor before the deadline.
The 2 August agreement is the only thing currently standing between the calendar and a lapse.

actors.name: Todd Blanche, Acting Attorney General
actors.actualPower: Directs how the Justice Department obligates its appropriated funds and negotiates for the department in Congress.
actors.constrainedBy: May only spend against purposes Congress appropriated for; the Senate can withhold the department's funding entirely.
actors.statedWants: Negotiated an agreement with holdout senators that removed the proposed $1.8 billion 'anti-weaponization' fund from pending spending legislation.
actors.leverageStatement: Trading the fund away unblocked the wider spending package.
actors.roleHere: Subject of the July hearing over the fund's legal authority, and party to the August deal that dropped it.

decisions.leverageStatement: Proposed the fund, defended it in hearing, then traded it away to unblock the bill.

actors.name: Mehmet Oz, Administrator, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
actors.actualPower: Decides whether a state's Medicaid spending complies with federal rules, and can withhold federal matching funds on that finding.
actors.constrainedBy: Medicaid matching is set in statute; a withholding decision is reviewable, and the Impoundment Control Act limits open-ended refusal to spend.
actors.statedWants: Blocked more than $800 million in federal Medicaid funding to California on the basis that some of the state's spending does not comply with federal Medicaid rules.
actors.leverageStatement: Holds the release of money already appropriated -- the clearest live example of the gap between Appropriated and Obligated.
actors.roleHere: The executive-branch side of the July withholding dispute with California.

decisions.leverageStatement: Holds the release. The money is appropriated and has not been rescinded; this office is why it has not moved.

actors.name: Gavin Newsom, Governor of California
actors.actualPower: Runs the state programme the withheld money funds, and can litigate the withholding.
actors.constrainedBy: Cannot compel release of federal funds; Medi-Cal covers roughly one in three Californians, so the state absorbs the gap in the meantime.
actors.statedWants: Argues California is serving its residents appropriately and that the funding decision is politically motivated.
actors.leverageStatement: Litigation and public pressure; no direct control over the disbursement.
actors.roleHere: The state on the receiving end of the withholding.

decisions.leverageStatement: Can litigate and publicise. Cannot compel disbursement, and carries the gap meanwhile.

actors.name: Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX)
actors.actualPower: Senior Judiciary Committee member; can compel testimony about how an agency is spending.
actors.constrainedBy: One vote of a hundred, and oversight questions do not by themselves stop a disbursement.
actors.statedWants: Pressed the Justice Department on where the 'anti-weaponization' fund's money comes from, how it is being spent, and who authorised it.
actors.leverageStatement: The hearing put the fund's legal authority on the public record, which is what made it tradeable three weeks later.
actors.roleHere: Opened the oversight thread that ended with the fund being dropped.

decisions.leverageStatement: Oversight put the fund's legal authority on the record, which is what made it tradeable.

actors.name: Sen. John Kennedy (R-LA)
actors.actualPower: A single senator's hold or withheld vote can stall a bill that needs sixty.
actors.constrainedBy: Cannot write the condition into law alone; it has to survive both chambers.
actors.statedWants: Said he would support anti-weaponization fund legislation only if it excludes people convicted in connection with the January 6 Capitol attack.
actors.leverageStatement: Attaching an eligibility condition to a vote he controls.
actors.roleHere: Named a condition on the DOJ fund the day before it was dropped.

decisions.leverageStatement: In a posture needing sixty votes, one senator's condition is close to a veto -- the fund was dropped the day after he set his.

actors.name: The Supreme Court of the United States
actors.actualPower: None over its own funding. It must ask Congress like any other agency.
actors.constrainedBy: The judiciary's budget is a line in an appropriations bill written by the other two branches.
actors.statedWants: Justices made a rare visit to Congress to request additional security funding.
actors.leverageStatement: Institutional standing and the visibility of an unusual appearance -- no procedural lever at all.
actors.roleHere: A reminder that the third branch is a supplicant in this process, not a participant.

decisions.leverageStatement: Funded by the same bills and with no role in passing them.

claims.text: The federal fiscal year begins on October 1 and ends on September 30.
claims.evidenceSummary: Set in statute at 31 U.S.C. § 1102; not a matter of practice or convention.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Already settled — the date is fixed by statute and would require an act of Congress to change.

claims.text: Congress is expected to enact twelve regular appropriations bills each fiscal year, one per subcommittee.
claims.evidenceSummary: The twelve-bill structure follows the standing subcommittee organization of the two appropriations committees.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Already settled, though the committees can and occasionally do reorganize their subcommittees.

claims.text: An authorization does not provide money; only an appropriation does.
claims.evidenceSummary: A foundational distinction in federal appropriations law, set out at length in the GAO Red Book.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Already settled as a matter of law.

claims.text: Money that has been obligated has not necessarily been spent.
claims.evidenceSummary: Obligation creates a liability to pay; the outlay follows separately and may be in a later fiscal year or never occur.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Already settled — the two stages are separately defined and separately reported.

claims.text: News coverage frequently describes a funding request using verbs that imply money has already been spent.
claims.evidenceSummary: Widely observed by budget analysts, but we have no systematic measurement of how often it happens, so this is an interpretation rather than an established fact.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: A coded sample of coverage of funding requests, counting how often a request is described with spending verbs.

claims.text: When appropriations lapse, agencies stop work because further obligation would be unlawful, not because cash has run out.
claims.evidenceSummary: Follows directly from the Antideficiency Act's prohibition on obligating in advance of an appropriation; the operational detail of what counts as an excepted activity varies by agency.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Agency-by-agency contingency plans showing the legal basis cited for each excepted activity.

claims.text: No money may be drawn from the Treasury except under an appropriation made by law.
claims.evidenceSummary: Article I, Section 9, Clause 7 of the Constitution, in force since 1789 and never amended.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Settled. It is the constitutional text.

claims.text: A bill that has passed only the House provides no money to anyone.
claims.evidenceSummary: Both chambers must pass identical text and the President must sign it (or a veto be overridden) before budget authority exists. Three of the stories logged in this window describe House-passed bills.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Settled. It is how bicameralism and presentment work.

claims.text: On 22 July 2026 the House passed a defense appropriations bill totalling roughly $1.15 trillion.
claims.evidenceSummary: Reported independently by The Washington Post and NPR within about six hours of each other. We do not hold the roll-call record or the bill text, so this rests on reporting rather than a primary document.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: The House roll-call vote record and the engrossed bill text on Congress.gov.

claims.text: The Pentagon package the House passed totals more than $1 trillion.
claims.evidenceSummary: True but superseded. This was the figure in the first reporting on 22 July; a more precise $1.15 trillion figure was reported the following morning. Retained because the imprecise number is what most readers saw first.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Already settled by the more precise figure. See house-passed-defense-bill-115t.

claims.text: The defense bill funds a U.S. military conflict with Iran.
claims.evidenceSummary: Reporting describes contingency provisions that could release additional funds if a conflict occurs. A contingency provision in a bill that has passed one chamber has released nothing. What is contested is not the text but whether 'funds' is the right verb for it.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Enactment of the bill and an apportionment or obligation record showing the contingency funds actually released.

claims.text: U.S. military action related to Iran has cost roughly $37.5 billion so far.
claims.evidenceSummary: An official figure disclosed by the Secretary of Defense and reported by The New York Times. It is a self-reported number from the department that spent it, with no published methodology and no independent audit, so it is strong but not confirmed.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: A GAO or CBO review, or a DoD cost report stating what is counted -- obligations, outlays, or both -- and over what period.

claims.text: The House passed a short-term continuing resolution on 22 July 2026.
claims.evidenceSummary: Reported by NPR. The Senate's vote was described as uncertain at the time.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: The House roll-call record and the resolution's text.

claims.text: The Senate agreement announced on 2 August 2026 has prevented a government shutdown.
claims.evidenceSummary: Senate leaders announced a bipartisan agreement. An announced deal is not enacted law: it still has to clear the Senate floor, pass the House and be signed. Nothing has been prevented until it is.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Enactment -- a signed bill, or the deadline passing without a lapse.

claims.text: The federal government will not experience a lapse in appropriations in this funding cycle.
claims.evidenceSummary: A deal exists in the Senate and both parties face election-season costs from a shutdown. Against that: Congress left for recess without a spending deal on 23 July, and objections to governing by repeated short-term patches were raised by senators of both parties.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: The funding deadline passing, either with enacted appropriations or with a lapse.

claims.text: A lapse now would be the third government shutdown since September of last year.
claims.evidenceSummary: Stated in NPR's 22 July reporting on the stopgap. We have not independently checked the count against the appropriations record.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: The dates of each lapse in appropriations since September 2025 from CRS or OMB.

claims.text: More than $800 million in federal Medicaid funding that California expected has been withheld by CMS.
claims.evidenceSummary: Both the federal administrator and the state governor confirm the withholding; they disagree about whether it is justified, not about whether it happened.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Settled as to the fact. The justification is a separate, open question.

claims.text: The California Medicaid withholding is politically motivated.
claims.evidenceSummary: Asserted by the state. No evidence of motive has been offered publicly by either side, and the federal justification on the record is a compliance finding about how California uses matching funds. Unsupported here means no evidence has been produced, not that the claim is false.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Internal deliberative records, or a pattern of comparable compliance findings against states treated differently.

claims.text: A proposed $1.8 billion DOJ 'anti-weaponization' fund was removed from pending spending legislation on 3 August 2026.
claims.evidenceSummary: Reported by NBC News following a deal between the Acting Attorney General and holdout senators. Consistent with the July Judiciary hearing and with Sen. Kennedy's stated condition the day before.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: The revised bill text showing the provision absent.

claims.text: The Justice Department has not publicly identified the appropriation that authorised its 'anti-weaponization' fund.
claims.evidenceSummary: A senior Judiciary Committee member asked in a public hearing where the money came from and who authorised it. We have found no published answer. Absence of a public answer is not proof there is no authority.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: A DOJ citation to the appropriation and apportionment, or the hearing transcript showing an answer was given.

claims.text: The Secretary of Defense submitted a classified supplemental funding request to Congress on 5 August 2026.
claims.evidenceSummary: Reported by Axios. The existence of the request is public; its contents are not, so the amount and purpose cannot be checked by anyone outside the cleared committees.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Confirmation from the defense committees, or an unclassified summary of the request.

claims.text: Coverage in this window describes money at a pre-outlay stage using verbs that belong to an outlay.
claims.evidenceSummary: Of the thirteen appropriations stories logged in the 23 days to 5 August 2026, two describe a bill that has passed one chamber as funding an activity: 'defense bill that could fund a potential Iran conflict' and 'Pentagon bill and budget blueprint for Iran war funding'. Neither bill was law and neither had released a dollar. Two of thirteen is a real rate, not the majority pattern this room originally implied.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: A larger coded sample across more outlets and a longer window, with the coding rule published.

claims.text: The Senate is acting to limit White House control over the release of federal science funding.
claims.evidenceSummary: Reported by The Washington Post as Senate action underway. We do not hold the vehicle, the text or its status, so what exactly is being limited is not established.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: The bill or amendment text and its stage.

claims.text: Supreme Court justices visited Congress in July 2026 to request additional security funding.
claims.evidenceSummary: Reported by The Washington Post and described as a rare appearance. A request only -- the first rung of the ladder.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: The judiciary's budget request document, or a committee record of the meeting.

claims.text: A government shutdown stops the federal government from paying interest on the national debt.
claims.evidenceSummary: Interest on the public debt is paid under a permanent, indefinite appropriation. It does not depend on the annual bills and does not lapse when they do. A shutdown and a default are separate events with separate legal triggers -- a lapse in appropriations stops discretionary operations, while a default would require Treasury to be unable to pay. This claim is kept in the ledger because it recurs every funding deadline.
claims.whatWouldSettleIt: Settled. See GAO's Principles of Federal Appropriations Law on permanent, indefinite appropriations.

stories.title: How an appropriation becomes spending
stories.dek: Five stages sit between a number in a budget request and money leaving the Treasury. Most coverage names only the first.
stories.howItWorksIntro: A federal dollar passes through distinct legal stages, each requiring a different actor to act. A request is a proposal from the executive branch. An authorization permits a program to exist. An appropriation provides legal spending authority. An obligation commits the money. An outlay pays it. Skipping any stage in a description of where money stands is not a simplification; it changes what is being claimed.

whyItMatters.text: Each stage has its own statutory basis, and an agency acting at the wrong stage is not merely early — it is in breach of the Antideficiency Act.
Different bodies control different stages, so 'the government decided to spend this' names no one in particular.
A request and an outlay can differ by the entire amount. Treating them as the same number overstates committed spending.
For anyone waiting on a federally funded service, only the outlay stage changes anything.
A newly announced figure almost always sits at the first stage, whatever the verb attached to it.
Funds can remain obligated but unspent across fiscal years, and some are eventually deobligated and returned.

stakeholders.impactSummary: Cannot obligate until OMB apportions the enacted appropriation, regardless of what the bill says.
Feel the obligation stage, when an award is made, rather than the appropriation stage.
Members of this group differ widely in how they read a funding figure, and some already distinguish the stages carefully. Treating them as one audience would overstate the confusion.

nextSteps.description: The regular appropriations bills are enacted before the fiscal year begins.
nextSteps.verificationCondition: Confirmed if all twelve regular bills are signed into law on or before September 30.

nextSteps.description: A continuing resolution carries agencies into the new fiscal year instead.
nextSteps.verificationCondition: Confirmed if a continuing resolution covering any of the twelve bills is enacted.

theme.title: Federal appropriations
theme.dek: How Congress decides what the federal government may spend, and the five stages between a proposed number and money actually leaving the Treasury.
theme.scopeStatement: The federal appropriations process itself: how spending authority is created, limited and executed. Covers the twelve regular bills, continuing resolutions, apportionment, obligation and outlay. Does not cover mandatory spending programs, tax policy, or state and local budgets.
inclusionRules: An official body acted — a committee markup, a floor vote, an enactment, or a veto.
A funding stage advanced for a specific appropriation.
A verified fact about the process changed.
A prediction about the process resolved.
A correction was issued to something we had published.
An authoritative body issued a new legal interpretation of the process.
exclusionRules: New commentary about an appropriation that was already logged.
Reporting that restates an earlier development without adding a fact.
Projections and estimates published without a stated method.
Coverage of mandatory spending, tax policy, or non-federal budgets.
theme.currentStatusSentence: Congress has not enacted full-year appropriations. A stopgap passed the House on 22 July, both chambers then left for recess without a deal, and Senate leaders announced an agreement on 2 August that has not yet cleared either chamber. Separately, more than $800 million already appropriated to California is being withheld by the executive branch. Of the thirteen funding stories logged here in the last 23 days, the largest number -- $1.15 trillion -- has passed one chamber and provided nothing to anyone.
theme.topUnresolvedQuestion: When Congress appropriates money and the executive branch declines to release it, who decides -- and what is an appropriation then worth?
theme.watchNext: Whether the Senate agreement announced on 2 August is enacted before the funding deadline, and whether the withheld California Medicaid funds are released, litigated, or formally rescinded.

essentialFacts.text: An authorization does not provide money. Only an appropriation does.
A bill that has passed only the House provides no money to anyone.
Money that has been appropriated has not necessarily been released, and money that has been obligated has not necessarily been spent.

terminologyNotes.note: We use 'spending' only for outlays — money that has left the Treasury. For earlier stages we name the stage: requested, authorized, appropriated, obligated.
We use 'lapse in appropriations' for the legal event and 'shutdown' for its operational consequence, because the two are frequently conflated and only the first has a statutory definition.
We avoid 'cut' without a baseline, since the same figure can be a cut against a request and an increase against the prior year. Where we use it, we state the baseline.
We use it only in quotation marks and only as the name the fund's sponsors gave it. Both sides of this dispute use the word for opposite conduct, so on its own it identifies nothing.
We do not call a contingency provision 'war funding'. A clause that would release money if something happens has not funded anything; we say what stage it is at.
We say 'withheld' for appropriated money an agency has not released. 'Blocked' and 'cut' both suggest the money is gone; withheld money is still appropriated and still owed unless rescinded.
An announced agreement between leaders is not enacted law. We name the stage -- announced, passed one chamber, enacted -- rather than saying a shutdown has been averted.

timeline.label: Budget and Accounting Act
timeline.description: Created a single executive budget request and established the predecessors of OMB and GAO.
timeline.whatWasKnownThen: Before this, agencies sent requests to Congress individually with no unified executive proposal.
timeline.textAlternative: 1921: the Budget and Accounting Act creates a unified executive budget request and the offices that became OMB and GAO.

timeline.label: Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act
timeline.description: Created the Congressional Budget Office and the budget resolution, and limited the President's ability to withhold appropriated funds.
timeline.whatWasKnownThen: Passed amid a dispute over impoundment; how far the new limits would bind future presidents was not yet tested.
timeline.textAlternative: 1974: Congress creates CBO and the budget resolution, and restricts presidential impoundment.

timeline.label: Fiscal year moved to October 1
timeline.description: The 1974 Act shifted the start of the fiscal year from July 1 to October 1 to give Congress more time.
timeline.whatWasKnownThen: The extra quarter was expected to make on-time enactment routine.
timeline.textAlternative: 1976: the fiscal year start moves from July 1 to October 1.

timeline.label: Antideficiency Act read to require shutdowns
timeline.description: Attorney General opinions concluded that agencies generally may not continue operating during a lapse in appropriations.
timeline.whatWasKnownThen: Earlier practice had often been to continue operating through short lapses; this interpretation changed that expectation.
timeline.textAlternative: 1980: legal opinions establish that a lapse in appropriations generally requires agencies to stop non-excepted work.

timeline.label: Justices ask Congress for security funding
timeline.description: Supreme Court justices made a rare visit to Congress to request additional security funding.
timeline.whatWasKnownThen: That the request had been made. No amount was reported and no bill carried it.
timeline.textAlternative: 14 July 2026: Supreme Court justices visit Congress to request security funding -- a request, at the first rung of the ladder.

timeline.label: Senate hearing questions the DOJ fund's authority
timeline.description: A senior Judiciary Committee member pressed the Justice Department on where a $1.8 billion 'anti-weaponization' fund's money came from and who authorised it.
timeline.whatWasKnownThen: That the fund existed and that Congress had not been given an accounting of it. Whether it rested on an appropriation was unresolved and remains so.
timeline.textAlternative: 15 July 2026: a Senate hearing puts the DOJ 'anti-weaponization' fund's legal authority on the public record.

timeline.label: House passes a stopgap and a $1T+ Pentagon bill
timeline.description: The House passed a short-term continuing resolution and, separately, a Pentagon package with a budget blueprint, before leaving for recess.
timeline.whatWasKnownThen: The Pentagon figure was first reported as 'more than $1 trillion'. The more precise $1.15 trillion figure came the next morning.
timeline.textAlternative: 22 July 2026: the House passes a stopgap and a Pentagon package, then leaves for recess.

timeline.label: Pentagon puts the Iran operation at $37.5 billion
timeline.description: The Secretary of Defense disclosed an estimated $37.5 billion cost for U.S. military operations related to Iran.
timeline.whatWasKnownThen: The figure was official and self-reported. No methodology was published, so whether it counted obligations, outlays or both was not stated.
timeline.textAlternative: 22 July 2026: the Pentagon discloses a $37.5 billion cost estimate for Iran-related operations.

timeline.label: CMS withholds $800M from California
timeline.description: Federal officials withheld more than $800 million in Medicaid funding California expected, citing compliance with federal matching rules.
timeline.whatWasKnownThen: That the money was withheld. The justification was disputed on the day and still is.
timeline.textAlternative: 22 July 2026: CMS withholds over $800 million in California Medicaid funds -- money appropriated but not released.

timeline.label: Congress leaves without a spending deal
timeline.description: Shutdown risk rose as Congress went into recess with no full-year agreement in place.
timeline.whatWasKnownThen: The stopgap had passed the House only. The Senate's path was uncertain.
timeline.textAlternative: 23 July 2026: Congress leaves for recess without a spending deal and shutdown risk climbs.

timeline.label: Senate deal, and the DOJ fund is dropped
timeline.description: Senate leaders announced a bipartisan funding agreement; separately, the $1.8 billion DOJ fund was removed from the pending legislation.
timeline.whatWasKnownThen: An announced agreement, not an enacted one. It still had to clear both chambers and be signed.
timeline.textAlternative: 2-3 August 2026: Senate leaders announce a funding deal and the $1.8 billion DOJ fund is dropped from the bill.

timeline.label: Now
timeline.whatWasKnownThen: This marker moves; it is not a historical event.
timeline.textAlternative: The present day, marking the right-hand end of the timeline.

developments.headline: Defense Secretary submits a classified supplemental funding request
developments.summary: Pete Hegseth sent Congress a classified request for additional Department of Defense funds, outside the open budget process. The existence of the request is public; its contents are not.
developments.whyItMatters: A classified request means the public and most members of Congress cannot see the amount or the purpose. Every later stage of the ladder -- authorized, appropriated, obligated, spent -- will be checkable only by the cleared committees, so the ordinary way of following the money does not work here.
developments.inclusionReason: An official body acted: the Secretary of Defense submitted a formal funding request to Congress.

developments.headline: Senate moves to limit White House control over federal science funding
developments.summary: Senate action is under way to constrain how far the executive branch can control the release of appropriated science funding.
developments.whyItMatters: This is a fight over apportionment -- the invisible step between Appropriated and Obligated. It decides whether an appropriation is an instruction to spend or a ceiling the executive may choose not to reach.
developments.inclusionReason: An official body acted, and the action bears on a legal interpretation of the process itself.

developments.headline: $1.8 billion DOJ 'anti-weaponization' fund dropped from the spending bill
developments.summary: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche reached agreement with senators who had been blocking the spending legislation over the fund. The provision was removed and the logjam broke.
developments.whyItMatters: The fund was never appropriated, so nothing was cut and nothing was rescinded -- a proposal was dropped. It is also the clearest illustration in this window of the purse being used as leverage: the department got its bill moving by giving up the provision.
developments.inclusionReason: An official body acted -- a negotiated change to pending appropriations legislation.

developments.headline: Senate leaders announce a deal to keep the government funded
developments.summary: The Majority and Minority Leaders announced a bipartisan agreement intended to prevent a shutdown. It still requires a Senate floor vote, House passage and the President's signature.
developments.whyItMatters: An announced deal changes the odds, not the law. Agencies are funded when a bill is signed; until then the deadline is unchanged and the risk is unchanged in kind, only in likelihood.
developments.inclusionReason: An official body acted -- Senate leadership announced a negotiated funding agreement.

developments.headline: Congress leaves for recess without a spending deal
developments.summary: Shutdown risk rose as both chambers went into recess with no full-year agreement, having passed only a stopgap in the House.
developments.whyItMatters: The calendar is the binding constraint in appropriations. Days spent in recess are days not spent on the twelve bills, and the deadline does not move.
developments.inclusionReason: An official body acted -- both chambers adjourned for recess with the funding bills unfinished.

developments.headline: House passes a $1.15 trillion defense appropriations bill
developments.summary: The House approved roughly $1.15 trillion in defense spending, including contingency provisions that would release further funds in the event of a conflict with Iran. The bill moves to the Senate.
developments.whyItMatters: This is the largest single number in the window, and it sits on the first rung. A bill that has passed one chamber has provided nothing; the contingency provisions have released nothing. Coverage describing it as funding a conflict is describing Requested with the verbs of Spent.
developments.inclusionReason: An official action: a chamber passed an appropriations bill.

developments.headline: CMS withholds more than $800 million in California Medicaid funds
developments.summary: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services blocked over $800 million California expected, saying some of the state's Medi-Cal spending does not comply with federal matching rules. The state disputes the finding.
developments.whyItMatters: This is the gap between Appropriated and Obligated made visible. The money exists in law and has not been rescinded; an agency is declining to release it. Medi-Cal covers roughly one in three Californians, so the gap is carried by the state in the meantime.
developments.inclusionReason: A funding stage failed to advance for a specific appropriation, by executive decision.

developments.headline: House passes a Pentagon package with a budget blueprint
developments.summary: The House approved over $1 trillion in Pentagon funding bundled with a budget framework designed to unlock reconciliation, plus a provision limiting stock trading by members of Congress.
developments.whyItMatters: The blueprint is the substantive move, not the dollar figure. Unlocking reconciliation would let one party pass further fiscal legislation in the Senate without the other's votes.
developments.inclusionReason: An official action: a chamber passed appropriations legislation and a budget resolution.

developments.headline: House passes a stopgap to keep the government open
developments.summary: The House passed a short-term continuing resolution extending current funding levels. The Senate's vote was uncertain. A lapse would be the third shutdown since September of last year.
developments.whyItMatters: A continuing resolution freezes last year's priorities. Programmes Congress voted to expand this year stay at the old level, and agencies plan in weeks rather than in a year.
developments.inclusionReason: An official action: a chamber passed funding legislation.

developments.headline: Pentagon puts Iran-related military costs at roughly $37.5 billion
developments.summary: The Secretary of Defense disclosed an official estimate of $37.5 billion for U.S. military operations connected to Iran.
developments.whyItMatters: This is the rarest kind of number in this room: money at the far end of the ladder rather than the near end. It is also self-reported by the department that spent it, with no published methodology stating whether it counts obligations, outlays, or both.
developments.inclusionReason: A verified fact about the process changed -- an official cost figure entered the public record for the first time.

developments.headline: Senate hearing questions the DOJ fund's legal authority
developments.summary: A senior Judiciary Committee member pressed the Justice Department on where the 'anti-weaponization' fund's money came from, how it was being spent, and who authorised it.
developments.whyItMatters: Appropriations control is exercised through questions like these as much as through votes. The hearing put the fund's authority on the record, which is what made it something the department could trade away three weeks later.
developments.inclusionReason: An official body acted -- a committee hearing examined an agency's spending authority.

developments.headline: Supreme Court justices ask Congress for security funding
developments.summary: Justices made a rare visit to Congress to request additional security funding for the judiciary.
developments.whyItMatters: The judiciary has no control over its own budget; it asks the other two branches like any agency. This is a request at the first rung, and nothing about it is funded.
developments.inclusionReason: An official body acted -- a formal funding request was made to Congress.

moneyItems.title: FY2027 defense appropriations bill
moneyItems.whatThisDoesNotMean: It does not mean $1.15 trillion has been provided to the Pentagon. The bill has passed one chamber. It is not law, no agency may obligate against it, and the contingency provisions tied to a possible Iran conflict have released nothing. If the Senate amends the topline, this figure changes.
moneyItems.decidesNext: The Senate, which must pass its own version and reconcile the difference.
exclusions: Contingency amounts that would only be released on a triggering event.
Any classified supplemental request, including the one submitted on 5 August 2026.
Mandatory military retirement and health spending, which is not in this bill.

comparisons.text: Roughly thirty times the $37.5 billion the Pentagon says Iran operations have cost so far.

comparisons.rejectionReason: Per-household framing on a figure that has passed one chamber implies a bill that has been sent. Nothing here has been appropriated, let alone collected.

moneyItems.title: U.S. military operations related to Iran, cost to date
moneyItems.whatThisDoesNotMean: It does not mean $37.5 billion has left the Treasury. The department did not say whether the figure counts obligations, outlays, or both, so it is placed at the more conservative rung. It is also not a total: operations are ongoing and the number is described as the cost so far.
moneyItems.decidesNext: Congress, if it requests a GAO or CBO review of the methodology.
moneyItems.estimateMethod: Self-reported by the Department of Defense with no published methodology. Placed at Obligated rather than Spent because the department did not state which it measured, and asserting the higher rung would claim more than the source does.
exclusions: Costs borne by other departments, including State and Veterans Affairs.
Future costs of equipment replacement and personnel care.

moneyItems.title: California Medicaid funds withheld by CMS
moneyItems.whatThisDoesNotMean: It does not mean the money was cut, and it does not mean it was rescinded. The appropriation stands; a federal agency is declining to release it on a compliance finding the state disputes. Nor is it a final figure — reporting describes it as more than $800 million.
moneyItems.decidesNext: CMS, which holds the release; or a court, if California litigates.
exclusions: State funds California may spend to cover the gap in the meantime.
Any future disallowance beyond the amount currently withheld.

comparisons.text: Medi-Cal covers roughly one in three Californians.

moneyItems.title: DOJ 'anti-weaponization' fund
moneyItems.whatThisDoesNotMean: It does not mean $1.8 billion was cut. The fund was a proposal in pending legislation and was removed before enactment, so nothing was rescinded and no programme lost money it had. Separately, the department has not publicly identified the appropriation behind the fund it already described as existing.
moneyItems.decidesNext: Nobody, unless the provision is reintroduced.
exclusions: Any existing DOJ spending described under the same name.

notApplicable.Authorized: The provision was removed from the legislation on 3 August 2026; no later stage will be reached unless it is reintroduced.

moneyItems.title: Supreme Court security funding request
moneyItems.whatThisDoesNotMean: No figure has been published. Justices asked Congress for additional security funding; we have not found an amount, and an empty ladder here means we do not know rather than that nothing was requested.
moneyItems.decidesNext: The appropriations subcommittee that writes the judiciary's line.
